top_choice_rationale: Anne Carson (P001) remains my first choice on the whole-authorship criterion. Her voice is highly distinctive and recognisable across decades and modes. Autobiography of Red recasts a fragmentary Greek source as a modern verse novel about desire and selfhood, and Nox makes elegy for a brother into a book whose form is part of the mourning. Eros the Bittersweet and the essays belong to the same practice: an inherited or broken form is reshaped until it carries present grief and desire. The citation should be scoped to original poetry, verse narrative and essays, anchored in the printed text, with Nox's physical form treated as an extension and the translations and classical versions treated as context. I rank Cărtărescu (P002) second. His project is more unified and can be stated in one sentence, and I hold the choice between unity of project and breadth of formal reinvention as a weighting I cannot fully resolve. P002 is clearly preferable to no award. My assessment rests on public knowledge, not fresh reading. Open uncertainties: whether Carson's later and performance-oriented books sustain the level of the central titles, how much a text-only reading loses of Nox, and, for Cărtărescu, translation fidelity and whether the late novels extend or repeat the earlier project. Her writing in English lowers a translation uncertainty but is not merit, and opening support counts and the number of explicit supporters are not evidence of merit.
recusal_note: none apparent from profile; the profile records no personal, institutional or collaborative tie to Carson or Cărtărescu. My own practice as a novelist is context only, and collegial service with other members is not evidence of a shared view.
